summary: Paul confronts the antinomian objection: if grace abounds where sin increases, should we continue in sin so that grace may multiply? 'May it never be!' Paul insists that baptism is a sacramental burial into Christ's death that severs the believer's union with the dominion of sin. Having died with Christ, believers are raised to walk in newness of life. Believers must not present their bodily members to sin, but present themselves to God as servants of righteousness leading to sanctification, culminating in eternal life.
whyItMatters: Romans 6 refutes the slander that free justification fosters moral lawlessness. It demonstrates that genuine salvation transfers the believer out of the enslaving kingdom of Sin into the liberating lordship of Christ.

context.author: Paul the apostle, with Tertius transcribing as amanuensis (16:22).
context.audience: Christian assemblies in Rome, encompassing returning Jewish believers and Gentile converts.
context.date: Circa AD 56–58, near the close of Paul's third missionary journey.
context.setting: Wintering in Corinth or Cenchreae, preparing to deliver the Jerusalem collection before journeying toward Spain.
context.literaryForm: Apostolic letter and theological treatise employing diatribe dialogue, scriptural catena, and pastoral exhortation.

outline.heading: Dead to Sin and United in Baptism
outline.note: Baptism unites believers with Christ in his death and burial so that, freed from sin's power, they walk in resurrection life, dead to sin and alive to God.

outline.heading: Presenting Your Bodies to God
outline.note: Believers are exhorted not to let sin reign in their mortal bodies, presenting their members as instruments of righteousness because they are under grace, not law.

outline.heading: From Bondage to Sin to Servants of God
outline.note: Obedience reveals allegiance: being freed from sin, believers became wholehearted servants of righteousness for sanctification.

outline.heading: Two Masters, Two Destinies
outline.note: Sin's fruit is shame and death, but God's fruit is holiness and his free gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus.

keyVerses.text: We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.
keyVerses.why: The theological definition of Christian baptism: a participation in Christ's burial and an ethical empowerment to live out his resurrected life.

keyVerses.text: Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
keyVerses.why: The crucial mindset of faith: believers are commanded to reckon as true what Christ has accomplished in breaking sin's jurisdiction.

keyVerses.text: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
keyVerses.why: A memorable contrast between the earned compensation of sin (spiritual and physical destruction) and the unearned charisma of God (everlasting life).

questions.question: What anticipated objection prompts Paul's question in verse 1?
questions.answer: Critics accused Paul's gospel of encouraging licentiousness: if more sin leads to more grace (5:20), why not sin continually to maximize God's glory? Paul rejects this premise with his forceful denial mē genoito ('may it never be!').

questions.question: How does baptism break the power of sin according to verses 3–7?
questions.answer: Baptism is not mere outward symbolism; it mystically incorporates the believer into Christ's corporate body, so that when he died to sin's ruling power, the believer's 'old self' died with him.

questions.question: What is the military meaning behind 'instruments' (hopla) in verse 13?
questions.answer: The Greek word hopla denotes weapons or armor. Paul envisions the human body as a contested battlefield: our limbs and faculties must not be surrendered as weapons for sin's unrighteousness, but dedicated as tools of God's justice.

questions.question: What does it mean that believers are 'not under law, but under grace' in verse 14?
questions.answer: Being 'under law' means living under the regime of legal condemnation without the Spirit's power; being 'under grace' places the believer under Christ's transforming reign, which achieves the moral righteousness the law demanded but could not produce.

questions.question: Why does Paul use the imagery of slavery in verses 16–19?
questions.answer: He uses a common Greco-Roman social reality to demonstrate that absolute human autonomy is a myth: every person is enslaved either to sin resulting in death, or to obedience resulting in righteousness and holiness.

questions.question: What was the 'form of teaching' (typos didachēs) delivered to the Romans in verse 17?
questions.answer: It refers to the apostolic catechetical summary of the gospel and basic Christian ethical instructions taught to new converts before baptism in the early church.

questions.question: How does Romans 6 guide modern believers dealing with persistent temptation?
questions.answer: It urges believers to base their identity on their baptismal union with Christ: instead of striving in self-effort, they are to count themselves dead to sin's claims and present their bodily habits daily to God.

glossary.def: The Christian initiatory washing (baptisma) enacting burial into Christ's death and emergence into resurrection life.
The ongoing moral purification and consecration of the believer to God (hagiasmos).
